source: Kitcher (1990) The Division of Cognitive Labor, J Philosophy 87(1):5-22
finding: Founding paper. Treats the best spread of scientists over rival approaches as a resource-allocation problem. Each approach has a return function: chance of success as a function of how many scientists work on it. A community of purely truth-seeking agents piles onto the most likely approach. A community that rewards credit can do better. Primary text not opened (paywalled, bot-blocked); content taken from secondary descriptions a02, a03, a28.
numbers: Return function gives P(success) from number of workers n. Kitcher's motivating example: phlogiston 0.51 vs new chemistry 0.49 confirmation before Lavoisier's experiment, swapped to 0.49 and 0.51 after (as quoted in a blog summary).
limits: Primary not read. Representative-agent model; success functions assumed known and objective.
agent_relevance: Core idea for S3 open mode: the best spread of attempts over directions is not 'all on the most likely one'. Code should allocate some attempts to directions with lower success chance but quick saturation.

source: Muldoon and Weisberg (2011) description of the MCR approach of Kitcher and Strevens
finding: Kitcher and Strevens share a 'marginal contribution/reward' (MCR) design. Each approach has a success function (Kitcher: return function) taking number of scientists and giving chance of success. Optimal spread is found by constrained maximisation. Classical rule 'take the most likely approach' misallocates: a harder approach with a low chance that saturates with few workers deserves a small team. Rewards for marginal contribution (Strevens' Marge) or first-to-finish (Priority) push a self-interested community near the optimum.
numbers: Example given: one approach has high success chance with a reasonable team; the other has low chance but reaches it with few workers. Under the 'most likely' norm, nobody picks the second.
quote: Classical epistemic norms are likely to cause scientists to misallocate themselves across projects.
limits: Summary of the two theories by their critics. Four idealisations: utility maximisers; a fixed set of predefined projects; everyone knows the current distribution of workers; everyone knows the true success function.
agent_relevance: Gives the allocation rule our code can use: assign the next attempt to the direction with the largest marginal gain in success chance, not the largest total chance.

source: Weisberg (forthcoming, 2010) New approaches to the division of cognitive labor, in New Waves in Philosophy of Science
finding: Three families of models: (1) MCR (Kitcher, Strevens), (2) epistemic networks (Zollman, Grim), (3) epistemic landscapes (Weisberg and Muldoon). Under MCR a credit-seeker weighs two things: the project's chance of success, and the chance of being first. The first pushes toward the best project; the second pushes toward projects with fewer workers. Strevens (2003) argues this tension is why science adopted the priority rule (winner takes all credit).
numbers: No simulation numbers; structural account of the three model families.
limits: Review by one of the model authors, so tilted toward the landscape approach. Read in the author's preprint (first 90 lines of text).
agent_relevance: The same two pulls (chance of success versus crowding) can be written as one score per direction: value times (1 - saturation). A cheap rule for the S3 allocator.

source: Strevens (2003) The Role of the Priority Rule in Science, J Philosophy 100(2):55-79
finding: Priority rule (all credit to the first finisher) explained as a reward scheme that spreads scientists over approaches. It gives a near-optimal spread without a planner. Strevens compares it with a marginal-contribution scheme (Marge). Primary not opened (paywalled; PDF sites blocked). Taken from a search summary and a02, a03.
numbers: No numbers recovered. Success functions left abstract; the form cancels in his analysis (per a02).
limits: Primary not read. Later critiques (search snippet only): Schneider and Rubin (2021) say priority disputes are idealised away; Heesen and Zollman say that under some plausible readings of the rule the model yields very bad results.
agent_relevance: For an agent there is no credit: the analogue is 'first to solve counts, repeats of the same idea earn nothing'. That supports a rule where repeating a direction already tried scores zero.

source: Strevens (2011) Economic approaches to understanding scientific norms, Episteme 8(2):184-200
finding: Abstract page only. Compares Strevens' own explanation of the priority rule with Max Albert's explanation of high methodological standards; both use economic methods but give different explanations. Reference list confirms the MCR lineage: Goldman and Shaked 1991, Kitcher 1990 and 1993, Brock and Durlauf 1999, Hull 1988.
numbers: None.
limits: Abstract and references only (paywalled).
agent_relevance: Lineage check only.

source: Muldoon and Weisberg (2011) Robustness and idealization in models of cognitive labor
finding: Agent-based re-implementation of Strevens' Marge scheme. With full information it reproduced Kitcher and Strevens qualitatively: few agents all take the easier project; more agents put a minority on the harder one; many agents put more on the harder one. Then they relaxed two assumptions and the result broke (a07, a08).
numbers: NetLogo 3.1.4; 500 agents; 2 projects with equal max success chance and equal payoff; project 2 harder; true easiness r = 0.02 and 0.03; logistic success function P = K/(1+e^(-rN)); agents on a 35 x 35 torus; each agent re-decides in random order, 10 rounds to reach equilibrium.
limits: Matches only qualitatively, because Strevens gives no numbers. Logistic function departs slightly from Strevens' decreasing-returns requirement.
agent_relevance: Allocation by marginal reward needs the allocator to see the true count per direction and the true success curves. Our code does see the history of directions tried, which is the one assumption that is true for a single agent with a ledger.

source: Muldoon and Weisberg (2011) Robustness and idealization in models of cognitive labor: distribution assumption
finding: When agents see only neighbours within a radius, the optimal spread fails. A majority pile on the easier project once the radius of vision is 12 units or less. Below 7 units no one works on the harder project. The break point depends on population density.
numbers: 500 agents, torus 35x35; radius <=12: majority on easier project; radius <7: zero on harder project.
limits: Local samples are biased because lab groups cluster on similar problems. Even a representative sample would not give raw counts without knowing field size. Only uniform random initial assignment was tested.
agent_relevance: A single agent with a full ledger has the full distribution, so this failure does not apply; it does apply to parallel attempts that cannot see each other (fresh contexts, S3).

source: Muldoon and Weisberg (2011) Robustness and idealization in models of cognitive labor: success function assumption
finding: When agents hold different beliefs about how easy each project is (same mean, rising variance), the community misallocates toward the easier project. With zero variance the result matches Kitcher and Strevens.
numbers: 500 agents; r beliefs drawn from a normal distribution with mean at truth (0.02 for project 1, 0.03 for project 2); variance increased in steps; error direction: toward the easier project.
quote: when this information is limited considerably, all scientists may chose to work on the easier project
limits: Authors argue success probabilities can only be subjective because a project is either right or wrong (phlogiston chance must be zero, DNA chance one). Exact variance values not recorded in the text read.
agent_relevance: Estimated success chances for directions are themselves noisy in an LLM. Allocation that trusts them will under-explore hard directions. Argues for a floor on exploration share per untried direction.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor: model
finding: Agent-based model. Scientists explore a landscape where x,y are research approaches and height is epistemic significance. Visiting a patch reveals its significance at no cost. Three movement rules: Control (HE, hill climbing with experimentation), Follower, Maverick. Agents leave markers on visited patches, standing for publications.
numbers: 101 x 101 toroidal grid = 10,201 patches; two Gaussian peaks (centres (25,25) amplitude .75 and (5,5) amplitude .7); significance jumps 0 to 50 at hill boundary; HE rule: 2% chance of random step on a plateau; NetLogo 4.0. Epistemic progress = share of patches with significance >0 visited.
limits: No research cost, no depletion of a visited patch, one fixed landscape with two smooth peaks, perfect lab skill. Authors say quantitative conclusions would be premature.
agent_relevance: Closest formal model of S3 open mode: directions are patches; history is the marker; 'maverick' is an allocator that moves to unvisited neighbours.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor: controls
finding: Independent hill climbers find the peaks slowly and unevenly. Adding scientists gives linear gains in coverage but only diminishing gains in finding the peaks.
numbers: 10 controls, 100 runs: both peaks found in 95/100; time to both peaks min 553, max 43,004 cycles; mean 6,075 (SD 8,518); median 2,553; 60% done within 4,000 cycles, 80% within 10,000. 20 controls: nearly always both peaks, median time halved. Gains small beyond 30 controls. Epistemic progress rises linearly with number of controls (400 controls: 0.24 at 500 cycles, 0.69 at 10,000). In the 5 failed runs everyone piled on one peak.
limits: Heavy-tailed completion times: luck dominates with small teams. 50,000 cycle cap.
agent_relevance: Independent samples (no coordination) already work as a baseline; the failure mode is all attempts landing on one peak, which the S3 history ledger prevents.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor: followers
finding: Followers move toward the best already-visited neighbour. They do worse than independent controls: they cluster, circle each other's trails, and stop.
numbers: 10 followers: zero runs found both peaks, 3% found one. 200 followers: one peak 60%, both 12%; when both found, mean 56 cycles. Epistemic progress: 400 followers 0.17; 10 followers 0.0065; 400 controls 0.24 at 500 cycles; fewer than 300 controls in 500 cycles match what 400 followers do in 1,000.
limits: Follower rule is one specific imitation rule using a Moore neighbourhood of 8 patches; 1,000-cycle limit.
agent_relevance: Imitating earlier successful attempts (copying a best-so-far, or voting on one model's samples) collapses diversity. Supports G4 and the fresh-context rule.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor: mavericks
finding: Mavericks (avoid visited patches, climb when no unvisited neighbour) beat controls and followers by a large margin on both finding peaks and covering the landscape.
numbers: 10 mavericks found both peaks in 99% of runs; 20 always. Mean time to both peaks: 80 cycles (10 mavericks), 37 (100), 33 (200). Progress after 200 cycles: 10 mavericks 0.10 (0.12 after 300 more cycles); 100 mavericks 0.55 (0.63 later); 200 mavericks 0.75 (0.80); 400 mavericks 0.90.
quote: pure populations of mavericks, who try to avoid research approaches that have already been taken, vastly outperform the other strategies
limits: Single smooth two-peak landscape; no cost of re-visits; mavericks are told which patches are visited without error. Later critics (a14, a15) show the size of the edge depends on landscape and rule.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S3: code keeps the history of directions tried and assigns unvisited ones.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor: mixed populations
finding: A few mavericks lift a large follower population, more than their own work explains, because they pull followers off stuck trails.
numbers: 400 followers + 1 maverick: progress +0.02 (t = 5.74, p < .001) and +232 approaches explored (t = 10.8). 400 vs 401 followers: ns (t = 1.47, p = .144). 100 followers 0.07 -> 0.15 with 10 mavericks (+214%); 400 followers 0.17 -> 0.28 (+165%). Gain from 10 mavericks: +0.08 at 100 followers, +0.11 at 400, so more than the mavericks' own work. Fixed 400 population with varying ratio: about 90% of approaches explored in 500 cycles at the best mix.
limits: Pure strategies mixed; same landscape. The best ratio is read from a figure; the text read is garbled there.
agent_relevance: Suggests a portfolio: most attempts follow the best lead, a minority are forced elsewhere. Matches the plan to mix a typical-answer-first attempt with forced untried ones.

source: Alexander, Himmelreich and Thompson (2015) Epistemic landscapes, optimal search, and the division of cognitive labor, Philosophy of Science 82(3)
finding: Challenge to Weisberg and Muldoon. A search strategy that deliberately seeks novel approaches need not be optimal. They say W&M did not show epistemic reasons for division of labour, and name the errors. They generalise the landscape model and conclude we should doubt the benefit of social learning in epistemically complex environments. Abstract page only (full text paywalled).
numbers: No numbers recovered.
quote: a search strategy that deliberately seeks novel research approaches need not be optimal
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: forced novelty seeking is not universally best. Fits G12: search only helps where there is a foothold; the allocator should not force exploration on every problem.

source: Thoma (2015) The epistemic division of labor revisited, Philosophy of Science 82(3)
finding: W&M's model implies it would be best if all scientists explored novel approaches, so no mixed population is needed. Thoma says this comes from implausible modelling choices and builds an alternative landscape model that does show benefits from division of labour, with one restriction. Abstract only.
numbers: No numbers recovered.
limits: Abstract only; the restriction is not stated in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Mixed portfolios (some imitators, some explorers) are favoured only if imitators add something (exploit what explorers found). In S3 this means a follow-up stage that refines a found lead, not only wide exploration.

source: Poyhonen (2017) Value of cognitive diversity in science, Synthese 194
finding: Extends W&M with heterogeneous learning heuristics. Result: social learning and cognitive diversity produce benefits only when the problem is hard enough. Abstract page only.
numbers: No numbers recovered.
limits: Abstract only (paywalled).
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for the S0 gate: spend the diversity budget only on hard classes (consistent with G12).

source: Bedessem (2019) The division of cognitive labor: two missing dimensions of the debate, European J Philosophy of Science 9
finding: Critique: DCL models miss (1) hierarchical levels of epistemic goals and (2) the nature of the object under study. So their use for research governance is limited. Abstract and notes page only.
numbers: None.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Warns against reading the models as policy rules. For us: models are design hints, to be checked by our own benchmark (G7).

source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers, PNAS 101
finding: Computational experiment: a random group of agents with different search heuristics beat a group made of the individually best agents, because the best agents are similar. 'Diversity trumps ability'.
numbers: Random value function on 2,000 points on a circle, values uniform [0,100]; each agent uses 3 look-ahead steps within l positions; 50 trials. Table: 10 agents, l=12: best 92.56 (diversity 70.98%) vs random 94.53 (90.99%). 20 agents, l=12: 93.78 (74.95%) vs 94.72 (91.46%). 10 agents, l=20 (6,840 possible agents): 93.52 (73.69%) vs 96.08 (94.31%). One run: best agent 87.3, 10 best average 87.1, 10 random average 85.6; groups 93.2 vs 94.7.
quote: a team of randomly selected agents outperforms a team comprised of the best-performing agents
limits: Gaps are 1 to 2.5 points. The theorem needs conditions (large pool, limited agent ability, diversity defined on heuristics). Reijula and Kuorikoski (2021, 2022) critique it, as cited in a19. Gap shrinks when group grows from 10 to 20.
agent_relevance: Selecting attempts for diversity of method rather than taking the top scorers can beat the top scorers when those are near-copies (G4).

source: Reijula, Kuorikoski and MacLeod (2023) The division of cognitive labor and the structure of interdisciplinary problems, Synthese 201:214
finding: Separates cognitive diversity (all work on the whole problem with different heuristics, as Hong-Page) from true division of labour (parts of the problem go to different workers). Splitting into blocks only pays if the problem is partly modular. Fully modular: split into single bits and solve fast. Fully non-modular: no split helps; only whole-problem search guarantees the optimum. Partly modular: the split matching the true block structure wins; wrong splits give weak signals.
numbers: Binary string problems, N = 4 worked example, simulations up to N = 12 and more; 50 repetitions over 50 landscapes; runs stop at 1,000 steps; N = 12 with two blocks of 6: the fully reductionist split leads early, then plateaus on a local maximum; the 6|6 split reaches the optimum; full-size search also reaches it but much more slowly. A 5|7 split looks almost as good so the error would not be noticed.
limits: Theoretical proof-of-concept, not an empirical test. Code at OSF (hw7zj).
agent_relevance: Second meaning of 'division': splitting a problem into subproblems is different from spreading attempts over alternatives. Our S3 open mode uses the second; decomposition lives in other operators.

source: Derex and Boyd (2016) Partial connectivity increases cultural accumulation within groups, PNAS 113
finding: Human experiment. Groups of 6 in a landscape where early innovations lock paths. Fully connected groups locked onto one path; partially connected groups explored different paths and then combined them.
numbers: 144 students (72 women, 72 men) in groups of 6 = 24 groups (12 per condition inferred from 91.7% = 11/12), 72 trials each, 6 ingredients, 56 triads. Level-3 innovation A3: 50% fully connected vs 91.7% partial; B3: 33.3% vs 66.7%; both A3 and B3: 0% vs 58.3%. Fully connected groups did better in the short run and peaked after about 35 trials. Participants adopted a newly found good ingredient within 2 trials in nearly 70% of cases.
quote: partially connected groups produce more diverse solutions, and this diversity allows them to develop complex solutions that are never produced in fully connected groups
limits: Small number of groups; one task; contacts were scheduled by the design. Differs from Mason and Watts 2012 on a different landscape (a21).
agent_relevance: Human evidence that copying the best lead collapses diversity while isolation preserves it; supports isolated attempts (S3) with later recombination.

source: Mason and Watts (2012) Collaborative learning in networks, PNAS 109
finding: Failed replication of the 'inefficient networks are better' prediction. In 256 web experiments with groups of 16 on a rugged landscape, efficient networks (short path lengths) did better, because searchers there explored more, not less. Networked groups beat independent searchers.
numbers: Groups of 16, 15 rounds, 8 network topologies, 232 sessions analysed. Peak found by at least one player in 138/232 networked sessions (59.5%). Score when peak found: networked 68 vs independent 39 (t = 92.5). Peak not found: 40.5 vs 32 (t = 35.6). Path length coefficient on score beta = -4.63, P about .01. Time for information to reach a node equalled path length 71% of the time.
limits: One landscape family (Perlin noise plus one Gaussian peak); players paid by individual score, each saw 3 collaborators' search history; any location could be jumped to, unlike Derex and Boyd.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: sharing information is not always harmful. When any location can be jumped to, shared history did not reduce exploration. For S3, showing the ledger of tried directions (not their scores) is the safe version.

source: Wu and O'Connor (2023) How should we promote transient diversity in science? Synthese 201:37: bandit models
finding: Review of model results on keeping diversity. Zollman's bandit models (from Bala and Goyal): less-connected networks reach the right consensus more often but slower; speed versus accuracy trade-off. Stubbornness, mild confirmation bias, individual exploration, and not sharing can all help the group, as they keep diverse practice alive.
numbers: No new numbers. Peptic ulcer case: Palmer (1954) persuaded the field bacteria cannot live in the stomach; overturned by Warren and Marshall (1983). Derex and Boyd 2016: groups of six; fully connected groups fail to reach top technologies. Mason and Watts 2012 find a general disadvantage to low connectivity. Gabriel and O'Connor 2021: mild confirmation bias beats none.
quote: Zollman describes this as a trade-off between speed and precision in epistemic communities
limits: Review, not primary. Dense versus sparse effect is sensitive to parameters (Rosenstock et al. 2017).
agent_relevance: Mixed record: diversity is good until evidence is decisive. Consistent with G1 (doubt on a signal) and G12.

source: Wu and O'Connor (2023) How should we promote transient diversity in science? Synthese 201:37: decision-theory framing
finding: The cost side. Diversity is harmful when too much effort goes to poor options. Bandit theory (Gittins index, epsilon-greedy that shrinks over time) gives the normative amount of exploration. None of the human-community mechanisms tracks the optimal rule. Rosenstock et al. (2017) argue that Zollman's advice to cut communication would create large inefficiencies, because transient diversity is needed mainly for hard problems.
numbers: No new numbers. Funding figure as quoted: industry about 72% of US R&D funding and about 75% of performance (Boroush).
limits: Review; the funders argument is policy, not directly transferable.
agent_relevance: Ties to sibling subfields on bandit exploration and exploration-exploitation. A decaying exploration rate is simpler and better founded than forced diversity.

source: Rosenstock, Bruner and O'Connor (2017) In epistemic networks, is less really more? Philosophy of Science 84
finding: Failed robustness test. The finding that sparse networks are better (Zollman 2007, 2010; Kummerfeld and Zollman) is not robust across parameter values. Per Wu and O'Connor and the SEP, with more nodes or larger gaps between arms the dense network's chance of a wrong consensus falls near zero. Abstract page plus secondary reading.
numbers: No numbers from the primary.
quote: previous results from epistemic network models ... showing the benefits of decreased connectivity in epistemic networks are not robust across changes in parameter values
limits: Abstract only; the detail above is secondary.
agent_relevance: Warns against hard-coding a degree of isolation. Tune on our own benchmark.

source: Zollman (2007) The communication structure of epistemic communities, Philosophy of Science 74
finding: Simulation of bandit-style learning on networks: in some contexts a community is more reliable when members are less aware of colleagues' experimental results; and there is a robust trade-off between reliability and speed. Abstract only.
numbers: No numbers from the primary.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Source of the idea that less information can help, behind fresh-context attempts (S3).

source: Zollman (2010) The epistemic benefit of transient diversity, Erkenntnis 72
finding: Division of labour can be kept in two ways: limit information, or give scientists extreme beliefs. With both, diversity never ends and agents fail to converge to truth. So the goal is transient, not permanent, diversity. Abstract page and notes only.
numbers: No numbers from the primary.
quote: the real epistemic goal is not diversity but transient diversity
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: S3 diversity should end: after the exploration phase, tests select (S4, S7).

source: Zollman (2013) Network epistemology: communication in epistemic communities, Philosophy Compass 8
finding: Survey: many different communication structures can be best; which is best depends on details of the problem. Abstract only.
numbers: None.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Another reason not to hard-code one structure.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, scientific knowledge and social epistemology, division-of-labour passages
finding: Describes Kitcher (1993): whether to follow a maverick strategy depends on its chance of success, how many peers pursue each strategy, and the reward; impure motives can still help progress. Strevens 2003: the priority rule yields divergent strategies. Muldoon and Weisberg reject uniform ideal agents. Zollman: cycle has highest chance of the right consensus, complete network has a non-trivial chance of lock-in; peptic ulcer example.
numbers: No numbers in the entry. Notes Rosenstock et al. (2017): with more nodes or bigger gaps in arm success rates, wrong consensus in the dense network drops near zero.
limits: Fetched through a summarising tool, so details are second hand; first 100,000 of 129,117 characters read.
agent_relevance: Quick map of the field for the schema notes.

source: Greaterwrong post, Research motivations and the division of cognitive labor (summary of Kitcher 1990)
finding: Blog summary of Kitcher 1990: credit-seeking scientists divide labour more rationally as a group than purely truth-seeking ones. Only worked number is Kitcher's phlogiston example (0.51 vs 0.49).
numbers: Phlogiston 0.51, new chemistry 0.49 before the 23 April 1787 experiment; swapped after.
limits: Blog; no equations or model results given; may be inaccurate.
agent_relevance: Context only; do not cite as the source for the model's numbers.
